tip: 'Pusing' covers both dizzy and stressed-out: 'kepala saya pusing' = my head is spinning.
'Gigi bungsu' = wisdom tooth, literally 'youngest-child tooth': 'dicabut' = gets pulled.
'Mata minus' = nearsighted, said with the number: 'minus saya bertambah' = my prescription got worse.
'Kacamata' = glasses, literally 'kaca' (glass) + 'mata' (eye): 'kacamata baca' = reading glasses.
'Masuk angin' ('wind got in') = the classic catch-all unwellness: chills, bloating, fatigue. Untranslatable.
'Jamu gendong' = 'jamu' sold by a walking vendor carrying bottles in a back sling ('gendong' = carry on the back).
'Panas dalam' ('inner heat') = folk ailment behind sore throats and canker sores; cooled with 'kelapa muda'.
'Asal' = as long as (condition): 'asal kulitnya tidak sampai terluka' = as long as the skin doesn't get hurt.
'Semoga cepat sembuh' is the standard get-well line, literally 'hopefully quickly recover'. 'Semoga' starts most wishes: 'semoga sukses', 'semoga lancar'.
'Titip salam' = pass greetings through someone: 'ibu titip salam' = mom sends her regards.
News and clinics shorten 'demam berdarah' to 'DBD' – three-letter abbreviations are everywhere in Indonesian, from 'KTP' to 'SD'.
'Kontrakan' = a whole house you rent, usually yearly; 'kos' = just a room: 'rumah kontrakan' = rented house.
'Anak kos' means a boarding-house renter, and it connotes a tight budget: 'masakan anak kos' = cheap cooking. Hence 'memasak sendiri' at the end of the month.
'Token' = prepaid electricity credit: 'beli token listrik' = buy a code and punch it into the meter.
'Mati lampu' = a power cut of any kind, not just the lamps: 'sedang mati lampu' = the power is out.
'DP' (say de-pe) = down payment: 'DP tiga juta' = a three-million down payment. Also called 'uang muka'.
'Bunga' = both flower and interest: 'cicilan tanpa bunga' = zero-interest installments.
An 'arisan' is a rotating savings club: everyone pays in each round, one member takes the whole pot, and the rotation runs until all have had a turn.
'Dikocok' = shaken up and drawn by lot: 'nama ibu keluar' = mom's name came out, she wins this round.
'Sembako' is short for 'sembilan bahan pokok' – the nine staple goods (rice, oil, sugar and so on). 'Harga sembako' = the price of the basics everyone tracks.
'Cair' (literally liquid) = money comes through: 'gajinya sudah cair' = the salary has landed.
'Ujung' means 'end'; doubled, 'ujung-ujungnya' is literally 'at its very ends' = 'it always ends up': 'ujung-ujungnya penuh barang yang tidak penting'.
Chili prices swing constantly and everyone tracks them – 'harga cabai naik lagi?' is genuine national small talk at any market stall.
'Ongkir' = 'ongkos kirim', the delivery fee; plain 'ongkos' is a transport fare: 'gratis ongkir' = free shipping.
'Demi' builds 'X by X' phrases: 'sedikit demi sedikit' = little by little, 'satu demi satu' = one by one. The doubling marks slow, steady progress.
'Tukang' = the ... guy, by trade: 'tukang parkir' = parking attendant, 'tukang galon' = the water guy.
'Kena' means 'get hit by' something unwelcome: 'kena biaya' = get charged a fee, 'kena hujan' = get rained on, 'kena macet' = get stuck in traffic.
On its own, 'tukang' means a handyman – the 'tukang' with his 'palu' and 'gergaji'. Add a trade and it names the specialist: 'tukang kayu' = carpenter.
'Ber-' + noun = 'to have/produce it': 'karat' rust, 'berkarat' rusty; 'debu' dust, 'berdebu' dusty.
One-syllable roots take 'menge-': 'cat', 'mengecat' = to paint; 'cas', 'mengecas' = to charge.
